competition_series: Formula Hybrid + Electric (Dartmouth, NH Motor Speedway) primary venue for driverless demonstrations 2023-2025; FSAE Michigan (SAE International) added a driverless component for the first time in 2026 under the new FSAE Driverless roadmap
summary: Carnegie Mellon Racing's driverless effort began informally in September 2021 as a student-led exploration of retrofitting a spare championship-winning electric FSAE chassis for autonomy, operating under the umbrella of Carnegie Autonomous Racing (CAR, founded January 2022, which also runs CMU's Indy Autonomous Challenge and F1TENTH programs). The team built its first driverless car, 19a (a converted 2019-generation electric chassis), reaching the first autonomous lap ever completed at a North American FSAE-family competition at Formula Hybrid + Electric on May 2, 2023 - but by the team's own account the vehicle was 'extremely unreliable' with a 'very rudimentary software stack.' A from-first-principles overhaul under VP of Driverless Ankit Khandelwal (2023-24) produced 22a, which grew the driverless roster from 6 to 30+ engineers, secured $30,000+ in in-kind LiDAR/GPU/GNSS sponsorship, implemented a GTSAM-based iSAM2 SLAM pipeline (developed with CMU Professor Michael Kaess), YOLOv8 perception, and a GPU-parallelized Monte Carlo MPC controller, and completed North America's first driverless track drive at Formula Hybrid + Electric 2024. The subsequent 24a (2024-25) was billed as CMR's 'first rules-compliant driverless car,' passing static technical inspection, and the 2025-26 car, 26X, became CMR's first vehicle to compete as both a traditional and autonomous entry, taking 1st place in Driverless Design at FSAE Michigan 2026 (the new roadmap's first year) and 1st overall at Formula Hybrid 2026. Public documentation is unusually strong for a North American team: CMR maintains an open technical-documentation site (cmr.red) and a public GitHub organization with a Docker-based development environment, though exact program-wide budget, added mass, and measured (as opposed to rule-target) EBS deceleration figures were not found.
dv_program_start: September 2021 - several Carnegie Mellon Racing students began informally exploring autonomously retrofitting an electric FSAE race car; formalized under the broader Carnegie Autonomous Racing (CAR) student organization founded January 2022.
first_autonomous_run_date: [uncertain] Not precisely dated in public sources. The first PUBLIC autonomous lap (19a) was at Formula Hybrid + Electric on May 2, 2023; some earlier private/parking-lot testing almost certainly preceded this (the perception lead's account cites 1,500+ development hours on 19a and an 8-person perceptions team), but no specific first-movement date was found.
first_dv_competition: Formula Hybrid + Electric, May 2, 2023 (19a) - first vehicle to complete a driverless lap at a North American FSAE-family competition, but this and the 2024/2025 Formula Hybrid appearances were exhibition/demonstration driverless laps, since no scored driverless class existed in North America at the time. The first entry into an officially SCORED FSAE Driverless class was FSAE Michigan 2026 (26X), where CMR placed 1st in Driverless Design - the new roadmap's first competition year.
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: [uncertain] approximately 20 months (September 2021 program start to the May 2023 Formula Hybrid exhibition lap), though true first autonomous movement (e.g., low-speed straight-line test) likely occurred somewhat earlier and is undocumented.
months_concept_to_first_competition: ~20 months to the first (exhibition) driverless competition appearance (Sept 2021 to May 2023); ~54 months to the first officially SCORED FSAE Driverless class entry (Sept 2021 to FSAE Michigan 2026).
months_to_first_scoring_run: [uncertain] approximately 54 months (Sept 2021 program start to FSAE Michigan 2026, the first year a scored driverless class existed in North America and CMR placed 1st in Driverless Design); no scored driverless dynamic (on-track) run result was found for CMR as of this research.

ramp_phases: Informally reconstructable from team materials: (1) 'concept/exploration' (Sept 2021-2022, informal retrofit exploration + CAR org formation); (2) 'simulation-first' (Spring 2022, Docker-containerized EUFS sim on ROS2 Galactic used before touching real hardware); (3) 'first retrofit / exhibition' (2022-2023, 19a built on a spare 2019 chassis, reaching an exhibition lap in ~20 months but described by the team as unreliable); (4) 'ground-up overhaul' (2023-2024, 22a, first-principles rebuild of software/electrical/mechanical with a 5x headcount increase); (5) 'rules-compliance' (2024-2025, 24a, focused on passing static technical inspection and formalizing EBS/shutdown-circuit/status-indicator hardware); (6) 'integration' (2025-2026, 26X, first single chassis built to run both driverless and human-driven, coinciding with the new roadmap's first scored North American driverless class).
what_slipped: The team's own retrospective on 19a (first-generation, 2023) states it was 'extremely unreliable' and had 'a very rudimentary software stack,' forcing an 'overhaul[ing of] the entire technical platform' in the very next generation (22a) rather than incremental iteration. This is the clearest documented schedule/quality slip: roughly 2 years elapsed between the first (unreliable) exhibition lap and the first vehicle described as 'rules-compliant' (24a, 2024-25), and a further ~1-2 years elapsed before the team's first scored driverless class placing (26X, FSAE Michigan 2026) - i.e., 'first autonomous lap' was reached quickly (~20 months) but 'competition-legal, scoring-capable driverless system' took roughly 3x longer (~54 months) from program start.
platform_prerequisites: Yes, and distinctively so: for every generation from 2023-2025 (19a, 22a, 24a), CMR retrofitted a SPARE prior-year electric competition chassis (e.g., 19a used the 2019-generation 'E' car) rather than the current season's competition car, avoiding direct resource contention with the traditional team. Only in 2025-26 (26X) did CMR build a single integrated chassis intended to run both traditional and driverless configurations in the same season - a structural change enabled by roughly 4-5 years of prior retrofit experience.
ebs_design: Hybrid pneumatic-actuation / hydraulic-application architecture consistent with DT.3.2: pneumatic pistons (fed by a large air tank through 800 PSI and 150 PSI regulator stages, an over-pressure protection valve set at 140 PSI, check valves, normally-open solenoids, and pressure sensors) directly actuate two dedicated EBS master cylinders; 3-way valves select the higher of manual vs. autonomous hydraulic pressure and feed the vehicle's existing brake calipers; 'holding chambers' provide stored-air redundancy if supply pressure is lost; manual release valves (mounted top-center, operable by anyone) release the brakes post-trigger; documented design intent is that 'if one part of this system fails, 50% of the braking functionality will still apply.' Design targets stated in team documentation (>10 m/s² average deceleration, ≤200ms reaction time from shutdown-circuit opening) match the FSAE rule minimums (DT.3.2.5) rather than being independently reported as measured/achieved values.
ebs_development_duration: [uncertain] Not documented; the EBS/pneumatic-hydraulic system as described appears to be a 24a-era (2024-25) formalization following the more basic 22a-era 'pneumatic emergency brakes triggered by the AIM board,' implying roughly 1-2 seasons of EBS-specific development, but no start/pass-test dates were found.
steering_actuation: Maxon EC 90 flat (Ø90mm, brushless, 400W, Hall-sensor) motor drives a timing belt/pulley system (1.8:1 ratio) turning a ball screw (5mm/rev lead, ~90% efficiency); a ball nut translates linearly, driving a CNC-milled aluminum carriage plate rigidly bolted to the steering rack's clevises; components mounted low near the chassis base plane to minimize cantilevered moment. Per DT.2.2 decoupling: no dedicated mechanical decoupling/clutch mechanism is used - the team instead relies on the low-lead, high-efficiency ball screw's inherent backdrivability plus minimal system friction to allow manual driver override without disconnection. PID-controlled; achieved lock-to-lock actuation in under 1 second and was validated over approximately 100 miles of on-track testing (22a, 2024).
brake_actuation: [uncertain] Distinct driverless SERVICE (non-emergency) brake actuation for normal autonomous driving is not separately documented; team materials describe braking primarily through the EBS pneumatic/hydraulic system integrated with the existing manual brake lines via 3-way valves, without a separately described lower-force 'normal driving' brake actuator.
sensor_mounting_packaging: [uncertain] Not documented in detail; team materials name the sensors (Hesai AT128 LiDAR, ZED2/ZED1 stereo cameras, Movella MTi-680G RTK GNSS/INS) but do not specify mounting locations (nose, roll hoop, main pod) or aero/packaging conflicts.
mass_added: [uncertain] not documented in any source found
chassis_impact: For 2023-2025 (19a/22a/24a), the driverless system was retrofitted onto a spare prior-season electric competition chassis each generation, implying repeated re-integration work rather than a persistent driverless-specific chassis. 26X (2025-26) marks the first ground-up single chassis intended to run both traditional and driverless configurations in the same season, a structural consolidation not attempted in earlier generations.
compute_platform: [uncertain] Team documentation refers only generically to 'the main CPU onboard the vehicle' and a GPU used for CUDA-based Monte Carlo MPC trajectory rollouts (128,000 samples/step); no specific compute module (e.g., Jetson model or x86 mini-PC) or secondary safety MCU model is named. The custom AIM PCB (STM32-based) functions as a safety-relevant interface/relay board alongside the main compute.
sensor_suite: Hesai AT128 hybrid solid-state LiDAR (primary depth/cone-position source); ZED2 (and earlier ZED1) stereo cameras (RGB imagery for cone color classification); Movella MTi-680G RTK GNSS/INS (position/orientation). Wheel-speed and steering-encoder sensor models are [uncertain, not documented]. Earlier-generation (19a, 2023) sensor suite was described only generically as 'stereo camera + LiDAR' without specific models.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: Remote Emergency Stop (RES) button press opens the safety circuit, disabling the tractive system and triggering the EBS relay. The custom AIM PCB physically houses the Driverless System Relay (mapped by the team to FSAE rule DT.4.1) and the Emergency Brake System Relay (mapped to DT.4.3). Three master switches coordinate operation: existing GLVMS and TSMS plus a new Driverless System Master Switch (DSMS) that gates driverless-mode selection and emergency-braking logic.
remote_stop_system: Gross Funk T53 transmitter paired with a GF2000i R98 vehicle-side receiver; the RES's remote-stop relay is hardwired in series with the vehicle's safety circuit; a bypass relay allows normal manual (non-driverless) vehicle operation when the DSMS is deactivated; the RES also carries the 'Go' mission-start signal.
status_indicators: Driverless System Status Indicator (DSSI) implemented as blue/yellow LED strips with a defined state machine: Off (no indication); Ready (yellow continuous - HV enabled, ready-to-drive, all safety checks passed); Active Mission (yellow flashing); Completed (blue continuous); Emergency (blue flashing, coincides with EBS actuation as the shutdown circuit opens). A separate Autonomous Mission Indicator (AMI) custom PCB with a rotary selector and LEDs displays/broadcasts the selected driverless mission over CAN to satisfy DO.1.4. No distinct ASSI naming was found; CMR's DSSI appears to serve the combined status/alert role described in DT.1.3/DT.1.4.
custom_pcbs: Autonomous Interface Module (AIM) - STM32-based; relays control actions from onboard compute to the vehicle over CAN, drives DSSI LEDs, conditions pneumatic brake-pressure sensor analog signals, performs driverless safety checks, and houses the Driverless System Relay and EBS Relay; firmware written in C, CAN debugging via PCAN. Autonomous Mission Indicator (AMI) - STM32-based, rotary selector + LEDs, satisfies DO.1.4 mission-selection/broadcast requirements. Design/fab/bring-up durations for either board are [uncertain, not documented].
software_stack: Distributed, publisher-subscriber ROS2 node architecture running on Ubuntu (Ubuntu 20.04 documented for the 24a-era software-architecture description). Automated boot sequence: LV system powers compute -> Ubuntu boots -> a cron job launches a tmux session that starts the pipeline -> ROS2 nodes initialize in a predetermined order -> a heartbeat monitor (5-second pulse) verifies node presence/publishing before allowing ready-to-drive, auto-restarting failed nodes. C++ and Python used across perception/planning; CUDA and Thrust used for GPU-parallelized MPC control. Development environment is Docker-first: the public 'driverless-docker' repository containerizes the OS, ROS2, Git integration, and CMR's full pipeline tooling for reproducible cross-machine development, with a dedicated build profile for the 26X vehicle generation and an optional (build-time-heavy) SLAM-package variant.
ros_version: Evolved across generations: ROS2 Galactic (Spring 2022, simulator-only, Dockerized EUFS sim); ROS2 Foxy (referenced in the 24a-era software-architecture documentation, Ubuntu 20.04); ROS2 Humble (referenced in the controls documentation's tech list: 'C++, ROS2 Humble, CUDA, and Thrust'). The exact distro-to-vehicle-generation mapping for 22a/24a/26X specifically is [uncertain]; current (26X-era) stack appears to run ROS2 Humble.
perception_approach: Two-stage LiDAR + camera pipeline. LiDAR (Hesai AT128): ground-plane fitting/removal followed by DBSCAN clustering to isolate cone-shaped point clusters as 3D centroids. Camera (ZED2/ZED1 stereo, RGB only): cone color classification via an Iterative-Closest-Point-based coloring module plus a reflectance-based regression model, feeding a YOLOv8 object detector (mAP 0.92, ~20ms inference after INT8 quantization from FP32) for blue/yellow/orange cone detection; the prior generation (19a) used YOLOv5 (92% detection accuracy) trained on an open-source FSAE cone dataset with Gaussian-blur, rotation, and hue/saturation augmentation. No specific maximum reliable detection range figure was found for either generation.
slam_localization_approach: iSAM2 (incremental Smoothing and Mapping) - a GTSAM-based factor-graph SLAM implementation developed in collaboration with CMU Professor Michael Kaess (a co-creator of iSAM2/GTSAM). The factor graph generates nodes for cone landmarks and vehicle poses, continuously solving a nonlinear optimization to refine both and control drift; described by the team as intended to progress the planner from midline paths toward minimum-time paths on subsequent laps. Predecessor research (2022, under Prof. John Dolan) implemented a from-scratch Extended Kalman Filter SLAM using Mahalanobis-distance-based maximum-likelihood data association, later ported from Python to C++ for a roughly 10 Hz runtime improvement, though it is [uncertain] whether this EKF-SLAM implementation was ever deployed on a competition vehicle versus being superseded by the iSAM2/GTSAM approach.
planning_approach: First-lap: midline path generated between currently-observed blue and yellow cones (unknown-track mode). Later laps: informed by the SLAM-built cone map. 22a-generation planner recast midline-finding as a binary classification problem solved via a nonlinear Support Vector Machine, using the SVM decision boundary (maximized margin between blue- and yellow-cone classes) as the track midline/path. The team's public GitHub organization also carries an active fork of TUM's 'global_racetrajectory_optimization' repository, indicating movement toward minimum-curvature/minimum-time trajectory generation beyond simple midline paths, though it is [uncertain] which vehicle generation has deployed this.
control_approach: GPU-parallelized (CUDA) Monte Carlo Model Predictive Control: samples 128,000 candidate control-action trajectories per control cycle, simulates each against a vehicle dynamics model, scores them with a cost function penalizing track-boundary proximity and kinematic-constraint violation, and outputs a weighted-average control action. Steering-actuator-level control uses a separate PID loop tuned to hit sub-1-second lock-to-lock response while avoiding overshoot.
simulation_tooling: Edinburgh University Formula Student (EUFS) open-source simulator, containerized in Docker (originally to solve an Ubuntu 16.04 dependency conflict) to run cross-platform on ROS2 Galactic (Spring 2022); models a VLP-16 LiDAR and ZED2 stereo camera and supports custom track generation. A peer-to-peer ROS2 node model let software subsystems be tested against simulated sensor data and ground-truth cone positions before deployment on real (expensive) hardware. Later-generation simulation tooling (for 22a/24a/26X specifically) is [uncertain] beyond the continued existence of a dedicated SLAM-enabled Docker build profile.
ci_cd_testing: GitHub Actions is used on the electrical/firmware 'monorepo' (consolidating DIM, HVC, DCM, RAM, VSM, and LV-BMS board codebases) to provide, in the team's own words, 'simple build tests and checks to have a weak guarantee that code will work.' No CI/CD pipeline was documented for the driverless perception/planning/control software specifically; the Docker-based development environment appears to substitute for formal CI on that side.
data_logging: DAQ-Live, a custom live-monitoring webpage (Node.js + ROS Web Bridge) streaming perception, path-planning, and raw sensor (camera/LiDAR/GPS) data for on-vehicle debugging. A separate 'PiDAQ' (Raspberry Pi Data Acquisition) repository exists in the team's GitHub organization, though its exact scope (traditional vs. driverless car) is [uncertain]. No rosbag/MCAP/Foxglove-specific workflow was documented.
open_source_repos: github.com/carnegiemellonracing (20 repos, 71 followers as of research date) - notably: driverless-docker (Dockerized ROS2 dev environment, actively updated), monorepo (electrical/firmware boards with GitHub Actions CI), PerceptionsLibrary22a (22a perception code), iSAM2_SLAM (forked SLAM implementation), driverless-ml-dev (MIT-licensed ML scripts), HesaiLidar_ROS_2.0 (CMR fork of the Hesai LiDAR ROS driver), global_racetrajectory_optimization (forked from TUM, minimum-time trajectory tooling), OpenBLT (CAN-based flashing). The team's public documentation site (cmr.red/driverless-docs and linked subdocs) is a genuinely useful, unusually detailed reference for other North American teams building a first driverless program, covering software architecture, perception, planning, controls, electrical, and mechanical subsystems end-to-end.
critical_path_items: (1) Acquiring a competent SLAM/state-estimation capability - the team explicitly routed around this via direct faculty partnership (Prof. Michael Kaess, a co-creator of iSAM2/GTSAM) rather than building it from a cold start, mirroring how European veteran teams lean on faculty labs; (2) headcount/expertise scaling - the documented 6-to-30+ engineer growth between the unreliable 19a and the redesigned 22a was treated by the team's own leadership as the primary lever for the platform overhaul; (3) rules-compliant safety hardware (EBS, shutdown circuit, DSSI, RES) - this was explicitly deferred to a THIRD generation (24a, 'first rules-compliant driverless car') after two generations focused on autonomy-stack proof-of-concept, indicating it was treated as a distinct, later-sequenced critical path rather than parallel work from day one.
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] No team-specific lead-time-in-weeks figures were found for any component. The team does note $30,000+ in in-kind LiDAR (Hesai AT128), GPU, and GNSS sponsorship was needed to equip 22a, implying these were treated as high-value/hard-to-source items secured via sponsorship rather than purchase, but no lead-time duration was documented.
first_dynamic_test_date: [uncertain] Not documented precisely; bounded above by the May 2, 2023 Formula Hybrid + Electric public exhibition lap (19a), with earlier private dynamic testing implied but undated.
testing_hours_before_first_comp: 1,500+ development hours reported for 19a (first generation, 2022-2023) by the team's Perceptions Captain; approximately 100 miles of on-track physical testing reported for the 22a steering system specifically (2023-2024). Total testing HOURS (as opposed to development hours) before either the 2023 or 2026 competition entries are [uncertain].
validation_strategy: [uncertain, partially documented] Documented elements include: static technical inspection (24a reportedly 'passed all static techs'), an EBS design with a stated dual-failure-mode redundancy target ('50% of braking functionality' retained on single failure), and extensive on-track mileage accumulation (~100 miles for the 22a steering system). No description of a formal safety case, FMEA process, or dedicated EBS pass/fail test event was found.
rules_compliance_challenges: [uncertain, inferred] The team's own generational labeling - 19a and 22a were not described as rules-compliant, while 24a was explicitly billed as CMR's 'first rules-compliant driverless car' - implies that achieving full DT-chapter compliance (EBS, shutdown circuit, DSSI/status indicators, RES) was a multi-generation, multi-year effort distinct from and slower than achieving basic autonomous driving capability. No specific rule number or inspection failure was documented as the hardest to satisfy.
tech_inspection_experience: [uncertain, partial] 24a (2024-25) is reported to have 'passed all static techs' at what team materials label 'FSAE Michigan 2024' (a date that is internally inconsistent with the car's '24a'/2024-25 naming and may reflect a labeling error in scraped team materials). No first-attempt pass/fail detail, specific items that failed, or year-over-year inspection history was found for 19a or 22a.
ebs_test_experience: [uncertain] No team-reported experience with a dedicated EBS dynamic test event (pass/fail, number of attempts, or measured deceleration/reaction-time result) was found. Team documentation states only the EBS's DESIGN targets (>10 m/s² average deceleration, <=200ms reaction time), which match the FSAE rule minimums under DT.3.2.5 rather than being reported as an independently measured, achieved result.
documentation_burden: [uncertain, inferred] The team maintains an unusually extensive public documentation site (cmr.red/driverless-docs plus six linked subsystem doc sets: perceptions, planning, controls, electrical, mechanical, software architecture) explicitly intended to help other teams start their own driverless programs, implying substantial internal documentation effort, but no hours/weeks figure or DSF/ASF-specific timeline was found.
dv_event_results: 2023: Formula Hybrid + Electric - first North American FSAE-family autonomous lap (19a), exhibition only, no scored driverless class existed. 2024: Formula Hybrid + Electric - first North American driverless track drive (22a), top speed near 30 mph at the event, exhibition only. 2025: 24a reported as CMR's 'first rules-compliant driverless car,' passing static techs; no scored dynamic result found. 2026: FSAE Michigan - 1st place, Driverless Design (26X), 4th overall (combined/traditional scoring, [uncertain] whether driverless dynamic points contributed); Formula Hybrid - 1st overall (26X), category composition [uncertain]. No confirmed driverless DYNAMIC (on-track, scored) event result was found for any year.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: 22a (2023-2024): 40 mph design/testing target reached during development and validated over ~100 miles of on-track testing of the steering system; approximately 30 mph reported as the top speed achieved during the actual Formula Hybrid + Electric 2024 track-drive demonstration.
ebs_deceleration_achieved: [uncertain] Only the DESIGN TARGET was found (>10 m/s² average deceleration, matching FSAE rule DT.3.2.5's minimum), not an independently measured/achieved value from an actual EBS test event.
perception_range_achieved: [uncertain] Not documented; team materials give algorithm performance (YOLOv8 mAP 0.92 at 20ms inference; YOLOv5 92% detection accuracy) but no maximum reliable cone-detection range in meters for either LiDAR or camera.
reliability_notes: The team's own account of 19a (2022-2023) states it was 'extremely unreliable,' the clearest documented reliability issue, though no specific DNF/cone-strike/off-course incident log was found. No reliability issues were documented for 22a, 24a, or 26X beyond the general narrative that each generation addressed shortcomings of the last.
top_mistakes: The team's own retrospective (from the 22a project lead) is that the first-generation vehicle, 19a, was built with 'a very rudimentary software stack' and was 'extremely unreliable,' which necessitated overhauling ALL of software, mechanical, and electrical systems in the very next generation rather than iterating incrementally - i.e., the implicit self-criticism is that the first generation under-invested in software/system robustness relative to the goal of simply achieving a public autonomous lap, creating rework in generation 2. Separately, rules-compliance (EBS, shutdown circuit, status indicators) was not tackled until a THIRD generation (24a), suggesting safety-system engineering was sequenced later than may be advisable for a team targeting actual scored competition entry rather than exhibition-only laps.
advice_for_new_teams: No direct first-person quotes addressed explicitly 'to new teams' were found, but the team's stated program goal - 'We want to see other teams start creating their own driverless programs' (carnegiemellonracing.org/driverless.html) - together with its decision to open-source both its software stack and a comprehensive, six-part technical documentation site (cmr.red/driverless-docs) functions as its primary form of advice/enablement to newer teams.
team_structure_dv: 2021-2022: informal, small exploratory group (headcount undocumented) within newly formed Carnegie Autonomous Racing (CAR, 90 CMU students across 10 departments, covering FSD + Indy Autonomous Challenge + F1TENTH + Learn-to-Race). 2022-2023 (19a): an 8-person Perceptions sub-team under a dedicated Perceptions Captain was documented; overall driverless headcount was approximately 6 by the end of this period. 2023-2024 (22a): grew from 6 to 30+ technical engineers under VP of Driverless Ankit Khandelwal, who also held the title 'Project Lead.' Current structure (per team.html, apparently 2025-26/26X era): Driverless subteam led by a VP of Driverless (Arya Lohia) reporting to CMR's Executive Board, with four Department Captains - Controls (Matthew Rao), Software Architecture (Nidhi Vadlamudi), Path Planning (Joshua Chong), and Perceptions (Raymond Jiang) - plus separate DV Electrical and DV Mechanical functions; described elsewhere as CMR's largest technical sub-team at 40+ (one source) to 60+ (another source) members.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain, inferred] No formally documented recruiting/onboarding process was found. The generational vehicle-naming convention itself (19a -> 22a -> 24a -> 26X, each with a public retrospective write-up by outgoing leadership, e.g., the 22a project lead's blog post) functions as an informal knowledge-transfer mechanism, and faculty mentorship (Profs. John Dolan and Michael Kaess) appears to have substituted for some year-over-year student-to-student transfer, particularly for SLAM.
budget_estimate: [uncertain, partial] $30,000+ in in-kind sponsorship (GPUs and 'state-of-the-art sensors' - LiDAR + GPS) was secured specifically for the 22a generation (2023-2024) per its project lead. No total driverless program budget or full per-year cash/in-kind breakdown across 2021-2026 was found.
recommended_sequence: Inferred from CMR's own generational history: (1) stand up a Docker-containerized, ROS2-based simulation environment (e.g., an open-source FS simulator) FIRST, before committing hardware budget, to enable cheap iteration; (2) pursue SLAM/perception expertise via direct faculty/lab partnership rather than building it cold, if such a partnership is available; (3) retrofit a SPARE prior-year competition chassis (not the current season's car) for the first driverless build, to avoid resource contention with the traditional team; (4) accept a rough, 'exhibition-only' first-generation vehicle as a deliberate milestone to prove feasibility and build team credibility/sponsorship, even if - as CMR's own account shows - it is unreliable; (5) fully re-architect software/electrical/mechanical systems in generation 2 once headcount and expertise have scaled, rather than continuing to patch generation 1; (6) treat rules-compliance hardware (EBS, shutdown circuit, DSSI, RES, custom safety PCBs) as its OWN sequenced milestone, distinct from and following basic autonomy-stack proof, budgeting a full additional generation/season for it; (7) only merge driverless into the primary competition chassis (a single dual-purpose vehicle) once the retrofit approach has matured across several generations.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: CMU's own pace - roughly 20 months from informal program start to a public (if unreliable) exhibition autonomous lap on a retrofitted chassis, with a small (6-person) team - is a strong existence proof that a first autonomous lap is achievable within a 24-month window for a comparably sized software-focused team. However, CMU's timeline also shows that 'rules-compliant' (24a, ~3.5 years in) and 'first scored competition placing' (26X, ~4.5-5 years in) each lagged the first exhibition lap by roughly 2-3 additional YEARS - i.e., the hardest, longest-lead parts of CMU's ramp were NOT the autonomy software stack (SLAM, perception, MPC), which a small team stood up relatively quickly with faculty help, but the safety/rules-compliance hardware (EBS, shutdown circuit, DSSI, custom PCBs) and headcount scaling needed to sustain iteration. A 24-month team targeting the new roadmap's 2026-2028 window should therefore: (a) budget EBS/shutdown-circuit/status-indicator engineering as a parallel, not sequential, workstream starting near month 1, given CMU visibly under-prioritized it in generations 1-2; (b) not assume that reaching a first autonomous lap implies being close to a scored, rules-compliant competition entry - CMU's own data suggests roughly a 2-3x time multiplier between the two; (c) leverage any available faculty/lab SLAM expertise directly, as CMU did with Prof. Michael Kaess, rather than building GTSAM/iSAM2-equivalent capability from scratch; (d) consider retrofitting a spare EV chassis rather than integrating into the primary competition car in year one, following CMU's own sequencing, only combining into a single dual-purpose vehicle once the driverless subsystems are mature.
